analogy.p: Imagine food as a huge piece of flat-pack furniture that is too big to get through the door (the gut wall). Workers with specific tools (enzymes) take it apart into small pieces that can be carried through. Each tool fits only one type of screw, just as each enzyme fits only one substrate, and a tool that is bent (denatured) no longer works. Bile is like a worker who first chops a large block into smaller chunks so the others can work on more surfaces at once. The analogy breaks down because enzymes are not used up and they are not alive.
analogy.t: A disassembly line in a factory

bullets: The digestive system is an organ system in which several organs work together to **digest and absorb food**.
**Glands** (the salivary glands and the pancreas) produce digestive juices containing enzymes.
The **stomach**, **liver**, **small intestine** and **large intestine** are the other main organs.
**Amylase** (a carbohydrase), **proteases** and **lipases** convert food into small soluble molecules.
**Bile** neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fat.
Higher tier: explain the effects of pH and temperature on enzyme action, and interpret graphs.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.2.2.1 and 4.2.2.2 ask you to describe the digestive system as an organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food, and to explain the role of **enzymes** and **bile** in digestion. You need to know the glands and organs involved, the three groups of digestive enzymes (carbohydrases, proteases, lipases), what each breaks down, the products, where each is made, and what happens to those products. Exams test this with labelled diagrams, tables, pH graphs and 4 to 6 mark explanations.

bullets: Starch is a large molecule made of many glucose units joined in a long chain.
Proteins are long chains of amino acids; lipids are made of three fatty acids joined to glycerol.
Small soluble molecules (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) can pass through the gut wall into the blood.
Digestion starts in the mouth (physical chewing and salivary amylase) and continues in the stomach and small intestine.
Absorption into the blood happens mainly in the **small intestine**.
core.p: Food contains large molecules such as **starch**, **proteins** and **fats** (lipids). These are **insoluble** and too big to pass through the wall of the digestive system into the blood. Digestion is the process of breaking these large molecules down into **small, soluble molecules** that can be absorbed. This is a chemical process, carried out by enzymes, so it needs the right conditions to be fast enough to keep us alive.

bullets: **Salivary glands**: produce saliva containing amylase, which starts to break down starch in the mouth.
**Stomach**: churns food with muscular walls; produces protease (pepsin) and hydrochloric acid.
**Liver**: makes bile, which is stored in the gall bladder.
**Pancreas**: produces amylase, protease and lipase and releases them into the small intestine.
**Small intestine**: produces amylase, protease and lipase; digestion is completed here and digested food is absorbed into the blood.
**Large intestine**: absorbs water from the undigested food, leaving faeces.
core.h: The organs of the digestive system and their jobs
core.p: Food travels along the gut: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and out through the anus. Along the way glands and the liver add chemicals. Each organ has a specific job, which makes the digestive system a very good example of how organs work together as an organ system. You should be able to label these organs on a diagram and state what each does.

bullets: **Substrate** = the molecule that the enzyme acts on.
**Products** = the molecules produced by the reaction.
Enzymes are proteins; their shape depends on how the chain of amino acids is folded.
The part of the enzyme where the substrate binds is the **active site**.
They are not used up in the reaction, so they can be used over and over again.
core.p: Enzymes are **biological catalysts**. A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself, and enzymes are **proteins**. Without them, the reactions of digestion would be far too slow at body temperature. Because enzymes are not used up, a small amount can break down a huge amount of substrate. Each enzyme works on a specific substrate, which is explained by its shape.

bullets: Step 1: the substrate collides with the active site.
Step 2: the substrate fits and an enzyme-substrate complex forms.
Step 3: the reaction occurs and the products leave the active site.
The enzyme is then free to bind with another substrate molecule.
Higher tier: the lock and key model is a simplified model; the real active site can change shape slightly (induced fit), but AQA only requires the lock and key idea.
core.h: Lock and key model: why enzymes are specific
core.p: Each enzyme has an active site with a particular shape. Only a substrate with a **complementary shape** fits, like a key in a lock. The substrate binds to the active site to form an **enzyme-substrate complex**, the reaction happens, and the products are released, leaving the enzyme unchanged and ready for another substrate. This is why one enzyme can only catalyse one type of reaction: amylase cannot break down proteins because protein does not fit its active site.

bullets: Human enzymes have an optimum temperature of about 37 °C.
Different enzymes have different optimum pH values: pepsin about pH 2, amylase about pH 7, small intestine enzymes about pH 8.
At low temperatures the enzyme is not denatured but the reaction is slow because few collisions occur.
A denatured enzyme cannot catalyse the reaction because the substrate no longer fits the active site.
On a rate-pH graph the curve is a peak, not a plateau: it falls on both sides of the optimum.
core.h: Effect of temperature and pH on enzymes (Higher tier detail)
core.p: Enzymes work fastest at their **optimum** temperature and pH. As temperature rises towards the optimum, particles move faster and collide more often with more energy, so the rate increases. Above the optimum, the bonds holding the protein in shape break and the active site changes shape: the enzyme is **denatured** and the substrate no longer fits. A pH that is too high or too low also denatures an enzyme in the same way. Denaturation is permanent.

bullets: Amylase: starch → maltose (simple sugars).
Made in the salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine.
The maltose is then broken down by other carbohydrases into glucose.
Glucose is small and soluble, so it is absorbed into the blood.
Test for starch: iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black (food tests are in the next spec point).
core.p: **Carbohydrases** convert carbohydrates into simple sugars. The example you must know is **amylase**, which breaks down **starch** into **maltose** (a sugar, which is then broken down into glucose by other carbohydrases in the small intestine). Amylase is made in the **salivary glands**, the **pancreas** and the **small intestine**. This explains why bread tastes slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time.

bullets: Proteins → amino acids.
Made in the stomach, pancreas and small intestine.
Pepsin (the stomach protease) has an optimum pH of about 2.
Hydrochloric acid also kills most bacteria taken in with food.
Amino acids are used to build new proteins, such as muscle and enzymes.
core.p: **Proteases** convert **proteins into amino acids**. They are made in the **stomach** (pepsin), the **pancreas** and the **small intestine**. Protease in the stomach works best in acidic conditions (about pH 2), which the hydrochloric acid in the stomach provides. This means pepsin would work poorly in the small intestine, where the pH is alkaline, and so the proteases made by the pancreas and small intestine work best at a higher pH.

bullets: Lipids → glycerol + fatty acids.
Made in the pancreas and small intestine.
Fatty acids and glycerol are small and soluble and are absorbed into the blood (lymph).
Lipids are used to build cell membranes and to store energy.
Lipase works at the surface of the fat droplets, so a large surface area speeds it up.
core.p: **Lipases** convert **lipids (fats and oils) into glycerol and fatty acids**. They are made in the **pancreas** and the **small intestine**. Lipid digestion makes the pH of the small intestine fall slightly because fatty acids are acidic, which is another reason bile needs to be alkaline. Lipids are large and insoluble in water, so lipase works much faster when bile has first broken the fat into small droplets.

bullets: Made in liver, stored in gall bladder, released into the small intestine.
Alkaline: neutralises stomach acid and gives the right pH for enzymes in the small intestine.
Emulsification is a physical change (not chemical): droplets get smaller but fat is not chemically changed.
Smaller droplets mean a larger surface area, so lipase breaks the fat down faster.
Bile contains no enzymes, so it does not digest the fat chemically.
core.h: Bile: made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder
core.p: **Bile** is made in the **liver** and stored in the **gall bladder** before being released into the **small intestine**. It has two jobs. First, it is **alkaline** and neutralises the hydrochloric acid that comes from the stomach, which gives the **alkaline conditions** that the enzymes of the small intestine work best in. Second, it **emulsifies fat**: it breaks large drops of fat into smaller droplets, giving a **larger surface area** for lipase to work on, so the fat is digested faster.

bullets: Glucose: used in respiration for energy; excess may be stored.
Amino acids: used to make new proteins such as enzymes, hormones and muscle.
Fatty acids and glycerol: used to make lipids such as cell membranes.
Products are carried in the blood plasma to cells around the body.
Link: the small intestine has villi, which provide a large surface area for absorption.
core.h: What happens to the products of digestion
core.p: After digestion the small soluble molecules are absorbed into the blood and carried around the body. The body uses them to **build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins**, and some of the **glucose is used in respiration** to release energy. This links the digestive system with the circulatory system (transport) and with the metabolism of the cells.

bullets: Link to 4.2.1: stomach is made of muscular, glandular and epithelial tissue.
Link to enzyme practicals: investigate the effect of pH on the rate of amylase (iodine test).
Link to 4.2.2.1: the digestive system as an example of an organ system.
Link to 4.5 homeostasis: the pancreas also makes insulin.
Always give both the substrate and the product, for example 'protease breaks down protein into amino acids'.
core.h: Linking and exam skills: putting it all together
core.p: The digestive system is a classic synoptic topic. It links organisation (tissues of the stomach), enzymes (rates and the required practical), transport (blood), and respiration (use of glucose). When you answer a long question, structure it by organ: name the organ, say what it produces or does, then say why that matters for digestion. Always use 'break down' with the substrate and product named.

exam: 'Name the enzyme / product' (1 mark): give exact pairs, for example amylase: starch to maltose; protease: protein to amino acids; lipase: lipids to glycerol and fatty acids.
'Describe the lock and key model' (2 to 3 marks): substrate has complementary shape to active site (1), forms enzyme-substrate complex (1), products released and enzyme unchanged (1).
'Explain why enzymes are specific' (2 marks): only one shape of substrate fits the active site (1), because they are complementary (1).
'Explain what happens at high temperature' (3 marks): bonds break (1), active site changes shape (denatured) (1), substrate no longer fits so rate falls (1).
'Explain the role of bile' (4 marks): made in liver, stored in gall bladder; alkaline so neutralises acid; gives optimum pH for enzymes; emulsifies fat to give larger surface area for lipase.
For pH or temperature graph questions: quote the optimum with units, then describe both sides of the peak; do not say 'the enzyme dies'.
For 'Why must food be digested?': large insoluble molecules cannot pass through the gut wall; they must be broken down to small soluble molecules.
Table questions: match enzyme, substrate, product and site exactly; use ticks only for places that make the enzyme.
6-mark answers: work through the system in order (mouth, stomach, pancreas and liver, small intestine) and name enzyme, substrate, product and conditions at each stage.
Use the phrase 'complementary shape' and 'active site' every time you explain specificity; examiners look for them.
Calculation of rate: rate = 1 ÷ time (or amount ÷ time); give units such as per second.

mistakes.r: Enzymes are proteins that are denatured by heat or the wrong pH; they are not alive.
mistakes.w: Enzymes are living things that get killed by heat.

mistakes.r: Enzymes are catalysts, so they are not used up and can be used again.
mistakes.w: Enzymes are used up in the reaction.

mistakes.r: State that the shape of the active site changes (it is denatured), so the substrate no longer fits.
mistakes.w: High temperature kills the enzyme's active site, so the substrate cannot fit.

mistakes.r: Bile emulsifies fat to give a larger surface area; lipase digests it. Bile contains no enzymes.
Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
mistakes.w: Bile is made in the gall bladder.

mistakes.r: Amylase: starch to maltose; protease: protein to amino acids; lipase: lipids to glycerol and fatty acids.
mistakes.w: Amylase breaks down protein / lipase breaks down starch.

mistakes.r: Most digestion and absorption happens in the small intestine; the large intestine absorbs water.
mistakes.w: Digestion happens in the large intestine.

mistakes.r: Bile neutralises the hydrochloric acid from the stomach so enzymes in the small intestine have an alkaline pH.
Hydrochloric acid gives the right pH for the protease (pepsin) and kills pathogens; the enzymes do the digesting.
mistakes.w: Stomach acid is there to digest food.

summary: AQA expects you to describe the digestive system as an organ system in which glands and organs work together to digest and absorb food, and to explain how amylase, proteases and lipases (biological catalysts working by the lock and key model) break starch, proteins and lipids into small soluble molecules, with bile neutralising stomach acid and emulsifying fat. It matters because digestion is the starting point for how the body obtains the molecules needed for growth and respiration, and it is heavily tested.

terms.d: A biological catalyst, made of protein, that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not used up.
The molecule that an enzyme acts on.
The part of an enzyme with a specific shape where the substrate binds.
A model in which the substrate fits the active site because it has a complementary shape.
When the shape of an enzyme's active site has changed so the substrate no longer fits.
The temperature or pH at which an enzyme works fastest.
An enzyme that breaks down carbohydrates into simple sugars; amylase is an example.
A carbohydrase that breaks down starch to maltose; made in salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins to amino acids; made in the stomach, pancreas and small intestine.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids to glycerol and fatty acids; made in the pancreas and small intestine.
An alkaline substance made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder that neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fat.
Breaking large drops of fat into smaller droplets, which increases surface area.
The breakdown of large insoluble food molecules into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.
An organ that produces digestive juices, for example the salivary glands and pancreas.
Acid made in the stomach that gives the right pH for protease and kills bacteria.

worked.ans: Enzymes have an active site of a specific shape (1). Starch has a shape complementary to the active site of amylase, so it binds and forms an enzyme-substrate complex (1), but protein does not have a complementary shape, so it cannot fit the active site (1).
worked.q: Explain why amylase breaks down starch but cannot break down protein. (3 marks)
steps: Identify the model: lock and key.
Say what is different about the shapes.

worked.ans: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder before it enters the small intestine (1). It is alkaline, so it neutralises the hydrochloric acid from the stomach (1) and gives the optimum pH for enzymes in the small intestine (1). It emulsifies fat into small droplets, giving a larger surface area so that lipase can break down the fat faster (1).
worked.q: Explain the role of bile in the digestion of fats. (4 marks)

worked.ans: 30 °C: rate = 20; 40 °C: rate = 40 (arbitrary units per second). The rate doubles because at the higher temperature the enzyme and substrate molecules move faster and collide more often and with more energy, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form per second (up to the optimum, above which the enzyme denatures).
worked.q: A student times how long amylase takes to break down all the starch in a mixture. At 30 °C it takes 50 s; at 40 °C it takes 25 s. Calculate the rate at each temperature (rate = 1000 ÷ time) and explain the change. (4 marks)
